Q000001.stem: A team compares a classic model with hand-crafted features against a deep learning model for classifying product photos. Why does the deep learning model need far more data but no manual feature design?

choices.text: It needs no training data because it is pretrained on rules
It stores every training image and looks them up
It uses fixed if-then rules written by experts

Q000001.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers that learn hierarchical features (edges, shapes, objects) directly from raw data. That removes manual feature engineering but requires large datasets and compute.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rules: that's rule-based systems.
• Lookup: that's memorization, not learning.
• No data: deep models learn from data.

Key takeaway: deep learning = learned features, lots of data.

Q000002.stem: A vendor says, 'We use XGBoost,' and another says, 'Download our churn model file.' Which statement distinguishes these correctly?

choices.text: Both are datasets used for training
XGBoost is a model; the file is the algorithm
Both are models; algorithm is a synonym

Q000002.explanation:
Why this is correct:
An algorithm is the learning procedure (such as XGBoost). A model is the artifact produced by running that algorithm on data: learned parameters that make predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synonyms: they're different.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Datasets: neither is data.

Key takeaway: algorithm + data → model.

Q000006.stem: A company wants one model to summarize reports, translate emails, and answer questions in natural language, without training separate models. What kind of model fits, and why?

choices.text: An LLM, a text foundation model for many tasks
A linear regression model trained on text length
An image classification CNN applied to documents
A rules engine with a dictionary for each task

Q000006.explanation:
Why this is correct:
LLMs are foundation models trained on massive text corpora. They can perform many language tasks such as summarization, translation, and Q&A through prompting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear regression: predicts numbers from features.
• Rules engine: brittle, one task at a time.
• Image CNN: for images.

Key takeaway: many language tasks, one model → LLM.

Q000011.stem: A company has 50,000 support tickets, each already tagged with a category, and wants to auto-route new tickets. What type of data and learning is this?
Q000011.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tickets with known categories are labeled examples. Training a classifier on labeled examples to predict categories for new tickets is supervised learning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlabeled/clustering: labels already exist.
• Time-series: not the structure here.
• Reinforcement learning: learns from rewards, not labels.

Key takeaway: known answers in the data → supervised learning.

Q000013.stem: A factory wants cameras to flag scratched products on an assembly line in real time, with minimal ML expertise. Which AI capability and service fit?

choices.text: Time-series forecasting with a regression model
Speech recognition with Amazon Transcribe on line audio
Computer vision, e.g., Rekognition Custom Labels

Q000013.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detecting visual defects is a computer vision task. Rekognition Custom Labels can train a defect detector from a modest number of labeled images without deep ML expertise.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comprehend: text.
• Transcribe: speech.
• Forecasting: predicts future values, not image defects.

Key takeaway: images → computer vision.

Q000014.stem: A company receives 20,000 emails a day in several languages and wants each tagged by sentiment and key phrases, with no ML team. Which service fits?
Q000014.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Comprehend is a managed NLP service that detects sentiment, key phrases, entities, and language in text, with no model training needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rekognition: images and video.
• Polly: text to speech.
• Textract: extracts text from documents.

Key takeaway: text analytics → Comprehend.

Q000016.stem: A streaming service wants each user's home page to show titles based on their history and similar users' behavior, updated as they watch. Which AI use case is this?

choices.text: Anomaly detection on each user's viewing history

Q000016.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Recommendation systems predict items a user will like from behavior and similar users. Amazon Personalize provides managed, real-time recommendations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anomaly detection: unusual patterns.
• Text extraction: documents.
• Speech synthesis: audio output.

Key takeaway: personalized suggestions → recommendation systems.

Q000018.stem: A retailer must predict next quarter's weekly sales per store, including seasonality and holidays, with a range of likely values. Which technique fits?

choices.text: Clustering of store locations by past sales volume

Q000018.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Forecasting uses historical values over time plus related factors (holidays, promotions) to predict future values, often with intervals to express uncertainty.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Classification: predicts categories.
• Clustering: groups items.
• Sentiment: text opinion.

Key takeaway: future numbers over time → forecasting.

Q000022.stem: A team deployed a model straight after training and it failed in production due to untested edge cases and changing data. Which pipeline order would have prevented this?

choices.text: Collect, prepare, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor

Q000022.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The ML lifecycle collects and prepares data, trains, evaluates before release, deploys, and then monitors to catch drift and trigger retraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Other orders: skip evaluation before deployment or put steps before their inputs exist.

Key takeaway: evaluate before deploy; monitor after.

Q000023.stem: A dataset has missing values, duplicate rows, and inconsistent date formats. The team also creates a 'days since last purchase' column. Which stage is this?

choices.text: Model monitoring after deployment to production

Q000023.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cleaning data and creating new features happen during data preparation and feature engineering, before training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deployment and monitoring: after training.
• Problem framing: before data work.

Key takeaway: clean and shape data before training.

Q000026.stem: Two data scientists retrain the same model a month apart and get different results, and nobody knows which code, data, or settings were used. Which MLOps principle is missing?

choices.text: Lower inference latency for the deployed endpoint
Repeatability via versioned code, data, and settings
A higher number of training epochs

Q000026.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Repeatability means runs can be reproduced because code, data, and configuration are versioned and pipelines are automated (for example, with SageMaker Pipelines).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scalability, latency, epochs: unrelated to reproducing results.

Key takeaway: version everything to reproduce results.

Q000029.stem: An ML team expects to go from 5 to 200 models and from thousands to millions of predictions per day. Which MLOps quality must the platform provide?

choices.text: Interpretability of a single model's predictions

Q000029.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scalability means the platform handles more models and higher volumes, for example through automated pipelines, managed endpoints, and auto scaling, without proportional manual effort.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Repeatability: reproducing runs.
• Interpretability: explaining predictions.
• Manual approval per prediction: doesn't scale.

Key takeaway: growth in models and traffic → scalability.

Q000032.stem: A RAG app answers poorly because each 80-page PDF is embedded as one vector. What should be done before embedding?

choices.text: Raise the temperature to add more detail
Fine-tune the LLM on each PDF
Tokenize each PDF into one very long vector
Chunk the documents into smaller passages

Q000032.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Chunking splits documents into passages sized for retrieval, so the search returns the specific relevant section instead of a whole document's diluted vector.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One long vector: the same problem.
• Fine-tuning: costly and not needed for retrieval.
• Temperature: randomness, not retrieval.

Key takeaway: good RAG starts with good chunking.

Q000033.stem: A search for 'cheap flights' should also find documents saying 'low-cost airfare'. What makes this possible?

choices.text: Exact keyword matching on the word cheap

Q000033.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Embeddings convert text into numeric vectors that capture meaning, so semantically similar phrases are near each other and vector search finds them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keyword match: misses synonyms.
• Sorting: unrelated.
• Temperature: generation randomness.

Key takeaway: meaning-based search → embeddings.

Q000035.stem: Older models processed text word by word and struggled with long-range references. Which innovation lets modern LLMs process sequences in parallel and relate distant words?
Q000035.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Self-attention lets each token weigh every other token in the sequence at once, enabling parallel processing and long-range context.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Decision trees, k-means, lookup tables: not the basis of modern LLMs.

Key takeaway: LLMs are built on transformers.

Q000037.stem: An insurer wants customers to upload a photo of car damage and ask 'How bad is this?' and receive a text answer, using one model. Which model type fits?

choices.text: A speech-to-text model with an image caption step
A multimodal model (image + text in, text out)

Q000037.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multimodal models accept multiple input types, such as images and text, and generate responses that reason over both.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Text-only: can't see the photo.
• Speech-to-text: audio.
• Forecasting: numbers over time.

Key takeaway: mixed inputs → multimodal.

Q000042.stem: A company uses one foundation model for summaries, emails, classification, and Q&A just by changing prompts. Which generative AI advantage is this?

choices.text: No need for any data governance

Q000042.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Foundation models adapt to many tasks through prompting or light customization, instead of one model per task.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deterministic: outputs vary.
• Guaranteed accuracy: hallucinations happen.
• No governance: still needed.

Key takeaway: one model, many tasks → adaptability.

Q000044.stem: A GenAI assistant cut support handling time by 30%, saving $400K a year, and cost $150K to build and run. Which metric expresses this?
Q000044.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ROI compares the benefit ($400K) with the cost ($150K), expressing business value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy: model quality.
• Tokens per second: speed.
• MTBF: reliability.

Key takeaway: business value → ROI.

Q000048.stem: A startup wants to try models from several providers through one API, with no servers or GPUs to manage, and keep its data out of model training. Which service fits?
Q000048.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock is a serverless service providing API access to foundation models from Amazon and third parties. Customer prompts and outputs aren't used to train the base models.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 GPUs: you manage infrastructure and models.
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Comprehend: fixed NLP tasks.

Key takeaway: many FMs, one serverless API → Bedrock.

Q000057.stem: A chatbot will handle 5 million requests a month with short answers, where a mid-size model already meets quality goals. Which factor should MOST drive the choice between that model and a larger one?

choices.text: The larger model's higher benchmark ranking
Cost per request at this volume

Q000057.explanation:
Why this is correct:
When quality requirements are met, cost at scale (tokens × volume) and latency usually decide. Bigger models cost more per token.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Popularity, branding, parameter count: not requirements.

Key takeaway: meet the quality bar at the lowest cost.

Q000059.stem: A support center serves customers in Korean, Spanish, and English and wants one foundation model. Which selection criterion matters MOST?

choices.text: The size of its training dataset only
Support for video input and long video summaries
Multilingual capability in the needed languages

Q000059.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The model must understand and respond well in all the required languages. Test it on real samples in each language.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Images or video: not needed.
• Training data size alone: doesn't guarantee language quality.

Key takeaway: choose models by the task's requirements.

Q000064.stem: An HR chatbot gives outdated leave policies because the policy changed after the model was trained. Which technique fixes this without retraining?

choices.text: Increase the temperature so the model explores newer policies
Pre-train a new model from scratch
RAG: retrieve current policies into the prompt

Q000064.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant, current documents at request time and adds them to the prompt, so answers reflect the latest information.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pre-training: very costly and still becomes outdated.
• Temperature: randomness only.
• Removing the system prompt: less control.

Key takeaway: current knowledge → retrieval, not retraining.

Q000068.stem: A prompt says 'Draft a reply to this customer,' and the output ignores the customer's order history. What should be added to the prompt?

choices.text: A random seed value so the reply stays consistent
Context: the relevant order history and details

Q000068.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Context is the background information the model needs, such as the customer's history, so it can produce a relevant response.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Max tokens: length only.
• Seed: repeatability.
• Shorter instruction: removes guidance.

Key takeaway: the model only knows what you give it.

Q000069.stem: A prompt includes an article and some examples but the model returns a list of keywords instead of a summary. Which prompt element is missing or unclear?

choices.text: The model version number and provider name

Q000069.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The instruction tells the model what to do, for example 'Summarize this article in 3 sentences.' Without a clear instruction, the model guesses the task.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Temperature, version, price: not prompt elements that define the task.

Key takeaway: say explicitly what task you want.

Q000072.stem: A zero-shot sentiment prompt mislabels sarcastic reviews. Which change is the simplest improvement, and what is it called?

choices.text: Fine-tune the model on millions of reviews

Q000072.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Zero-shot gives no examples. Few-shot prompting adds a handful of labeled examples, including tricky ones such as sarcasm, which often improves accuracy quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning: heavier than needed first.
• No instructions: worse.
• Image model: wrong modality.

Key takeaway: zero-shot → few-shot before customization.

Q000079.stem: A startup is considering building its own foundation model from scratch. What does this pretraining step involve?

choices.text: Training on massive data with huge compute
Fine-tuning an existing model on 1,000 records
Adding a few examples to a prompt

Q000079.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pretraining trains a model from scratch on very large, broad datasets to learn general patterns. It requires enormous compute and cost, so most companies start from existing foundation models.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Few-shot prompts, fine-tuning, and retrieval: all build on an existing pretrained model.

Key takeaway: pretraining is rarely the right starting point for a business.

Q000080.stem: A law firm wants a model to write in its specific clause style consistently. It has 5,000 labeled examples of prompts and ideal outputs. Which customization fits?

choices.text: Pretraining a new model from scratch

Q000080.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning further trains a pretrained model on task-specific labeled examples, teaching consistent style and format.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pretraining: unnecessary and costly.
• Temperature: randomness.
• Guardrails: restrict content; they don't teach style.

Key takeaway: consistent task-specific behavior from labeled examples → fine-tuning.

Q000085.stem: A team builds a defect detector with only 500 images by starting from a model already trained on millions of general images. What is this approach called?
Q000085.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer learning reuses knowledge from a model trained on one task or dataset to improve learning on a related task with less data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reinforcement learning: rewards.
• Clustering: no labels.
• Rules: no learning.

Key takeaway: reuse learned knowledge → transfer learning.

Q000089.stem: A model gives correct but rude answers. Reviewers rank pairs of responses, and a reward model trained on those rankings guides further training. What is this technique?
Q000089.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback uses human preference rankings to train a reward model, which then steers the model toward preferred behavior such as helpfulness and tone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Few-shot: examples in prompts.
• Continued pretraining: more unlabeled domain data.
• Augmentation: expands training data.

Key takeaway: align with human preferences → RLHF.

Q000091.stem: Automated scores rate two chatbot versions equally, but customers prefer one. Which evaluation approach captures tone, helpfulness, and brand fit?
Q000091.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Human reviewers judge subjective qualities such as helpfulness, tone, and appropriateness that automatic metrics miss. Bedrock supports human evaluation jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Token counts, file sizes, GPU use: not quality measures.

Key takeaway: subjective quality → human evaluation.

Q000092.stem: A team compares three models on its task. Why use a standardized benchmark dataset alongside its own tests?

choices.text: Consistent, repeatable comparison on the same tasks
It guarantees the best benchmark model wins in production
It trains the models to be more accurate
It removes the need for any business testing

Q000092.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Benchmarks give a common, repeatable basis for comparison. They don't replace testing on the company's own data and goals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guaranteed production win: benchmarks may not reflect your use case.
• No business testing: still needed.
• Training: benchmarks evaluate, they don't train.

Key takeaway: benchmarks compare; your data decides.

Q000100.stem: A chatbot's BLEU and ROUGE scores improved, but leadership asks whether it helps the business. Which metrics answer that?

choices.text: Task completion rate and cost per interaction
Model parameter count and context window size
BLEU score on a new dataset

Q000100.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Business metrics such as task completion, containment, customer satisfaction, and cost per interaction show whether the application delivers value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Perplexity, BLEU, parameters: technical measures.

Key takeaway: measure outcomes the business cares about.

Q000102.stem: A medical FAQ bot must give factually correct answers grounded in approved content. Which responsible AI dimension is this?
Q000102.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Veracity and robustness concern producing correct, truthful outputs, supported by grounding and evaluation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Controllability: steering behavior.
• Privacy: protecting data.
• Fairness: equitable outcomes.

Key takeaway: correctness → veracity.

Q000103.stem: A model answers correctly for clean inputs but fails badly when users add typos or slight rephrasing. Which responsible AI property is lacking?
Q000103.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Robustness means stable, reliable behavior under variations in input, including noise or small changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transparency and explainability: understanding the model.
• Governance: oversight processes.

Key takeaway: stable under messy inputs → robustness.

Q000107.stem: A model scores 98% in training but 70% on new data, and worst on a small demographic group with few training examples. What is happening?

choices.text: Too much training data for the model's size

Q000107.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Overfitting means the model memorized training data and generalizes poorly. Groups with few examples suffer most, which also creates fairness issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Underfitting: poor on training data too.
• Perfect generalization: contradicted by results.
• Too much data: usually reduces overfitting.

Key takeaway: high train, low test → overfitting; check subgroups.

Q000110.stem: A bank's assistant must refuse to give investment advice, even when asked indirectly. Which Bedrock Guardrails feature fits?

choices.text: Denied topics with a definition and examples

Q000110.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Denied topics describe subjects the application must avoid (with a definition and sample phrases), detecting them even when phrased indirectly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Violence filters: harmful content categories.
• Profanity: specific words.
• Grounding: hallucination checks.

Key takeaway: off-limits subjects → denied topics.

Q000113.stem: A regulator asks how a model works, what data trained it, and its known limits. Which responsible AI concept is this, and which AWS artifact helps?

choices.text: Latency; document it in CloudWatch dashboards
Scalability; document it in Auto Scaling policies
Cost; document it in AWS Budgets

Q000113.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transparency means stakeholders can understand a model's workings, data, and limitations. Model Cards document intended use, training data, evaluation, and risks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scalability, latency, cost: operational topics.

Key takeaway: transparency → documented models.

Q000116.stem: A company wants to build a product on an open-source foundation model. Which step best supports responsible and legal use?

choices.text: Skip evaluation because the model is popular
Assume open source means no restrictions
Review the license and model card

Q000116.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Open models come with licenses that may restrict use cases or require attribution, and documentation describes training data and limits. Both must be reviewed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No restrictions: many licenses have conditions.
• Removing attribution: may violate terms.
• Skipping evaluation: popularity isn't fitness.

Key takeaway: read the license and model card before building.

Q000120.stem: A company labels chatbot replies 'Generated by AI' and explains which data sources are used. Which principle does this serve?

choices.text: Faster response time for labeled replies
Transparency to users about AI content

Q000120.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Disclosing that content is AI-generated and its sources helps users calibrate trust, which is part of transparency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Robustness, cost, speed: unrelated to disclosure.

Key takeaway: tell users when they're dealing with AI.

Q000124.stem: A company trains a custom model on SageMaker AI. Which task is the company's responsibility under shared responsibility?

choices.text: Physical security of AWS data centers

Q000124.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS secures infrastructure. The customer controls access (IAM), protects data (encryption and classification), and configures the service securely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data centers, hypervisors, network hardware: AWS responsibilities.

Key takeaway: customers secure what they put in and who can access it.

Q000130.stem: A customer's security review asks for AWS's ISO 27001 and SOC 2 reports. Where should the company get them?
Q000130.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS's compliance reports and agreements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
• Config: resource compliance in your account.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: AWS's own compliance reports → Artifact.

Q000133.stem: A team wants ongoing recommendations on cost savings, security settings, fault tolerance, and service limits across its account. Which service fits?
Q000133.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor checks accounts against best practices in cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, and service limits, with recommendations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Artifact: compliance reports.
• Macie: sensitive data.
• Audit Manager: audit evidence.

Key takeaway: best-practice recommendations → Trusted Advisor.
